title: Problem Overview and Imports
content:
Erdős Problem #238: For $c_1, c_2 > 0$, can we find $> c_1 \cdot \log(x)$ consecutive primes $\le x$ with all gaps $> c_2$? Proved for small $c_1$ (Erdős); general case OPEN.

The formalization imports from Mathlib: Nat.Prime.Nth for prime enumeration, Filter.Basic for asymptotic statements, and SpecialFunctions.Log for logarithms.
mathContext: $\text{mainConjecture}: \forall c_1 > 0, \forall c_2 > 0, \forall^\mathrm{f} x \in \mathrm{atTop}, \exists k > c_1 \cdot \log(x), \exists m, \text{allPrimesLeX}(m,k,x) \wedge \text{allGapsLarge}(m,k,c_2)$.

title: Prime Enumeration
content: `nthPrime(n) = Nat.nth Nat.Prime n` gives the $n$-th prime (0-indexed in Lean: nthPrime 0 = 2, nthPrime 1 = 3, etc.). `primeGap(n) = nthPrime(n+1) - nthPrime(n)` is the gap between consecutive primes. These are noncomputable since `Nat.nth` uses classical choice.
mathContext: $p_n = \text{Nat.nth Prime } n$, $g_n = p_{n+1} - p_n$. By the PNT, the average gap $\bar{g}(x) \sim \log x$.

title: Consecutive Prime Sequences
content:
`consecutivePrimes m k : Fin k → ℕ` gives $k$ primes starting from $p_m$. `allPrimesLeX m k x` requires all primes in the sequence $\le x$. `allGapsLarge m k c₂` requires all $k-1$ consecutive gaps exceed $c_2$.

The use of `Fin k` for indexing ensures the sequence is exactly $k$ primes, and `Fin (k-1)` for gaps captures exactly the $k-1$ adjacent pairs.
mathContext: $\text{consecutivePrimes}(m, k, i) = p_{m+i}$ for $i \in \{0, \ldots, k-1\}$. The gap condition: $\forall i < k-1, c_2 < p_{m+i+1} - p_{m+i}$.

title: The Main Conjecture (OPEN)
content:
For ALL $c_1, c_2 > 0$, eventually $\exists$ run of $k > c_1 \cdot \log(x)$ consecutive primes $\le x$ with all gaps $> c_2$. Uses `Filter.Eventually` ($\forall^\mathrm{f}$ in atTop) for 'sufficiently large $x$'.

The universality over both $c_1$ and $c_2$ is what makes the conjecture hard: even as the run length requirement grows (larger $c_1$), all gaps must simultaneously exceed the threshold $c_2$.
mathContext: $\text{mainConjecture} \equiv \forall c_1 > 0, \forall c_2 > 0, \forall^\mathrm{f} x \in \mathrm{atTop}, \exists k, m, c_1 \cdot \log(x) < k \wedge \text{allPrimesLeX}(m,k,x) \wedge \text{allGapsLarge}(m,k,c_2)$.

title: Negation of Conjecture
content: If the conjecture fails: $\exists c_1, c_2 > 0$ such that for infinitely many $x$, no run of $c_1 \cdot \log(x)$ consecutive primes $\le x$ has all gaps $> c_2$. This explicit negation is used in `conjecture_vs_negation` to prove $\text{mainConjecture} \Rightarrow \neg\text{conjectureNegation}$.
mathContext: $\text{conjectureNegation}: \exists c_1 > 0, \exists c_2 > 0, \forall N, \exists x > N$, no valid $(k,m)$ pair exists.

title: Erdős's Partial Result (Axiom)
content:
For any $c_2 > 0$, there exists sufficiently small $c_1 > 0$ (depending on $c_2$) making the conjecture hold. The quantifier swap ($\exists c_1$ vs $\forall c_1$) is the gap between known and open.

This is the deepest axiom in the formalization: Erdős's proof uses the PNT to show that for small $c_1$, the expected number of qualifying runs in $[1, x]$ tends to infinity, then applies a second-moment argument.
mathContext: $\text{erdos\_partial\_result}: \forall c_2 > 0, \exists c_1 > 0, \forall^\mathrm{f} x \in \mathrm{atTop}, \exists k, m, c_1 \cdot \log(x) < k \wedge \ldots$ Compare with the conjecture: $\forall c_1 > 0, \forall c_2 > 0, \ldots$

title: Prime Number Theorem Context
content:
Two axioms providing PNT context:

`average_gap_grows`: For any $c_2 > 0$, eventually there exists a gap $> c_2$ among primes $\le x$. This is a consequence of the average gap $\sim \log x \to \infty$.

`prime_number_theorem_asymptotic`: $\pi(x) \sim x/\log x$, formalized as $|\pi(x)/(x/\log x) - 1| < \varepsilon$ eventually. Uses `Finset.filter Nat.Prime` for the counting function.
mathContext: $\pi(x) = |\{p \le x : p \text{ prime}\}| \sim \frac{x}{\log x}$. Average gap: $\frac{x}{\pi(x)} \sim \log x$, so for fixed $c_2$, most gaps exceed $c_2$ when $x$ is large.

title: Run Length Analysis (Proved)
content:
`maxRunLength(x, c)` = $\sup\{k : \exists$ run of $k$ consecutive primes $\le x$ with all gaps $> c\}$. Uses `sSup` (supremum in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$).

`conjecture_implies_run_growth` (**proved theorem**, formerly axiom): If the main conjecture holds, then $\text{maxRunLength}(x, \lceil c_2 \rceil) > c_1 \cdot \log(x)$ eventually. Proof uses `le_csSup` with a `BddAbove` bound derived from strict monotonicity of prime enumeration (`n \le p_n`).

title: Heuristic Analysis (Proved Theorem)
content:
`large_gaps_eventually_dominate`: For large $x$, gaps exceeding $c_2$ become common. This is a PROVED theorem (from `average_gap_grows`), not an axiom.

The heuristic argument: if fraction $1 - o(1)$ of gaps exceed $c_2$, then the probability of $k$ consecutive large gaps $\approx (1 - o(1))^k$. For $k = c_1 \cdot \log(x)$, this is roughly $e^{-o(\log x)} \to 1$. Making this rigorous requires controlling gap correlations — the key difficulty.
mathContext: If gaps are independent with $P(g_n > c_2) = 1 - o(1)$, then $P(\text{run of length } k) \approx (1-o(1))^k \approx 1$ for $k = O(\log x)$. But prime gaps are NOT independent — this is a heuristic only.

title: Cramér's Conjecture (Context)
content:
Cramér (1936) conjectured that the maximal prime gap below $x$ is $O((\log x)^2)$. This is much stronger than needed for Problem 238 but provides context: if gaps are bounded by $(\log x)^2$, they're typically much smaller, making long runs of large gaps plausible.

Formalized as a Prop definition: $\exists C > 0$ such that eventually all gaps between primes $\le x$ satisfy $g_n \le C (\log x)^2$. Cramér's conjecture itself remains open.
mathContext: $\text{cramersConjecture}: \exists C > 0, \forall^\mathrm{f} x, \forall n, p_{n+1} \le x \Rightarrow g_n \le C (\log x)^2$. The best unconditional bound is Baker-Harman-Pintz (2001): $g_n \ll p_n^{0.525}$.

title: Structural Theorems (Verified)
content:
Two verified theorems demonstrating the logical structure:

`partial_weaker_than_full`: mainConjecture implies the partial result (trivially: instantiate $c_1 = 1$). This confirms the full conjecture is strictly stronger.

`conjecture_vs_negation`: mainConjecture implies $\neg$conjectureNegation. Proof by extracting witnesses from the filter and reaching a contradiction with the negation. This 12-line proof uses `Filter.Eventually`, `mem_atTop_sets`, and structural unpacking.
mathContext: The key step in `conjecture_vs_negation`: from $\forall^\mathrm{f} x$, extract $x_0$ via `mem_atTop_sets`, find the negation's $x > x_0$, and derive a contradiction from simultaneously having and not having a qualifying run.

title: Summary and Status
content:
`erdos_238_summary` packages the known results: Erdős's partial result and the problem statement. `erdos_238_status` records the status as a string.

The formalization has 3 axioms (erdos_partial_result, average_gap_grows, prime_number_theorem_asymptotic) and 7 verified theorems/lemmas including the proved conjecture_implies_run_growth.
